chunks: I entered upon Abu al-Abbas at al-Hira, so he said, 'O Abu Abdillah, what do you say regarding the fast today?' So I said, 'That is up to the Imam — if you fast, we fast, and if you break the fast, we break the fast.' So he said, 'O boy, bring me the food!' So I ate with him.
and I know, by God, that it was a day from the month of Ramadan. So my breaking the fast for a day and making it up is easier upon me than that my neck be struck off, and God not be worshipped.

key_terms.أَيْسَر: Easier; comparative of يسر (yusr), ease — indicating the lesser of two burdens under necessity
key_terms.الإِمَام: Here used rhetorically — the Imam deferred to the governor as 'the leader', a diplomatic maneuver
key_terms.الصِّيَام: Fasting (sawm/siyam); the obligation of abstaining from food and drink during Ramadan
key_terms.تَقِيَّة: Dissimulation (taqiyya); permissible concealment of one's true belief or practice under duress to preserve life
key_terms.قَضَاء: Make-up; compensatory fasting performed after Ramadan for days missed

ai.seo_question: Did Imam al-Sadiq break his fast out of taqiyya when with the Abbasid governor?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) narrates a tense encounter with Abu al-Abbas, the Abbasid caliph or governor at al-Hira, who questioned him about whether to fast on a day of ambiguity. The Imam deflected by deferring the decision to the ruler himself, then ate with him despite knowing inwardly it was Ramadan — an act of dissimulation (taqiyya) to preserve his life. The Imam's concluding remark reveals the jurisprudential calculus: breaking a fast with qada (make-up) is a minor matter compared to execution, which would prevent God from being worshipped through the Imam's continued existence and guidance.
